title: Sequences & Number Patterns
description: Arithmetic and geometric sequences, term-to-term and position-to-term rules, special sequences, visual patterns, and the method of differences.

notes.heading: What is a Sequence?
notes.body:
A sequence is a list of numbers written in a definite order. Each number in the list is called a term. Sequences appear everywhere — in timetables, music rhythms, and nature.

📌 Definition
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers called terms.

    $$2, 4, 6, 8, 10, \dots$$

    $2$ is the first term, $4$ is the second term, and so on. The three dots ($\dots$) mean the sequence continues in the same way.

🔑 Key Concept
Every sequence follows a rule or pattern. To describe a sequence you need to know:
1. The first term
2. How each term is related to the one before it, or how each term is related to its position number

💡 Worked Example
Write the first five terms of the sequence that starts at $5$ and adds $3$ each time.

  Step 1: Start with the first term
    First term $= 5$

  Step 2: Add $3$ repeatedly
    $5 + 3 = 8$
    $8 + 3 = 11$
    $11 + 3 = 14$
    $14 + 3 = 17$

  Step 3: Write the sequence
    $$5, 8, 11, 14, 17$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A sequence must have an order — $1, 3, 5$ is different from $5, 3, 1$
• Terms are often written as $u_1, u_2, u_3, \dots$ or $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$
• The position of a term tells you where it sits in the list

⚠️ Common Misconception
A sequence is not the same as a set. In a set, order does not matter; in a sequence, order is everything.

illustration.caption: A sequence follows a rule. The term-to-term rule tells you how to get the next term. The nth term formula lets you find any term directly from its position.

notes.heading: Term-to-Term Rules
notes.body:
The term-to-term rule tells you how to move from one term to the next. Finding this rule is the first step in understanding almost any sequence.

📌 Definition
A term-to-term rule is an instruction that takes you from one term to the next term.

    Examples:
    • 'add $4$'
    • 'subtract $3$'
    • 'multiply by $2$'
    • 'divide by $2$'

🔑 How it Works
Look at the difference or ratio between neighbouring terms. If the same amount is added or subtracted each time, the sequence is called an arithmetic sequence.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Adding each time
Find the term-to-term rule for $7, 12, 17, 22, 27$.

  Step 1: Work out the differences
    $12 - 7 = 5$
    $17 - 12 = 5$
    $22 - 17 = 5$
    $27 - 22 = 5$

  Step 2: State the rule
    The rule is 'add $5$'.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Subtracting each time
Find the term-to-term rule for $40, 34, 28, 22, 16$.

  Step 1: Work out the differences
    $34 - 40 = -6$
    $28 - 34 = -6$
    $22 - 28 = -6$
    $16 - 22 = -6$

  Step 2: State the rule
    The rule is 'subtract $6$' (or 'add $-6$').

⚠️ Common Mistake
Only checking the first two terms. Always check at least three differences before deciding the rule is correct.

notes.heading: Continuing Sequences and Finding Missing Terms
notes.body:
Once you know the term-to-term rule, you can continue a sequence or fill in a missing value.

🔑 Key Concept
To continue a sequence, keep applying the rule. To find a missing term, use the terms on either side to find the rule and then check it works.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Continuing a sequence
Continue the sequence $9, 14, 19, 24, 29$ for two more terms.

  Step 1: Find the common difference
    $14 - 9 = 5$
    $19 - 14 = 5$
    Rule: add $5$

  Step 2: Continue the pattern
    $29 + 5 = 34$
    $34 + 5 = 39$

  ✅ Check: The differences are still $5$, so the answer is correct.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Finding a missing term
Find the missing term in $11, \underline{\quad}, 25, 32, 39$.

  Step 1: Use the known terms to find the rule
    $32 - 25 = 7$
    $39 - 32 = 7$
    Rule: add $7$

  Step 2: Fill in the missing term
    $11 + 7 = 18$

  Step 3: Check the next step
    $18 + 7 = 25$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Look at the differences between terms first
• If the difference is constant, the sequence is arithmetic
• Always check your answer by continuing the pattern

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to check that the missing term fits on both sides. A term must work with the term before it AND the term after it.

notes.heading: Position-to-Term Rules (the nth Term)
notes.body:
A position-to-term rule lets you find any term without writing out the whole sequence. In IB and MYP, this is often written using the letter $n$ for the position number.

📌 Definition
The $n$th term rule is a formula that gives the value of the term in position $n$.

    For an arithmetic sequence with first term $a$ and common difference $d$:

    $$n\text{th term} = a + (n - 1)d$$

🔑 How it Works
If the common difference is $d$, the rule will contain $dn$ (a multiple of $n$). Adjust the constant so the first term is correct.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Finding a term from the rule
The $n$th term of a sequence is $4n + 3$. Find the $6$th term.

  Step 1: Substitute $n = 6$
    $4(6) + 3$

  Step 2: Calculate
    $24 + 3 = 27$

  ✅ Check: The sequence begins $7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27$, so the $6$th term is $27$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Finding the rule from a sequence
Find the $n$th term rule for $6, 10, 14, 18, 22$.

  Step 1: Find the common difference
    $10 - 6 = 4$
    Start with $4n$

  Step 2: Find the adjustment
    When $n = 1$, $4n = 4$, but the first term is $6$
    $6 - 4 = 2$

  Step 3: Write the rule
    $$n\text{th term} = 4n + 2$$

  ✅ Check: For $n = 3$, $4(3) + 2 = 14$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The coefficient of $n$ is the common difference for arithmetic sequences
• The constant adjusts the formula to give the correct first term
• You can use the rule to find ANY term, no matter how far along

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing $4n + 6$ instead of $4n + 2$ because you forget to compare with $n = 1$. Always test your rule on the first term.

notes.heading: Special Sequences
notes.body:
Not every sequence adds or subtracts the same amount. Some important sequences appear again and again in mathematics.

🔑 Key Concept
Recognising special patterns helps you predict terms quickly.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Square numbers
The sequence of square numbers is:

    $$1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, \dots$$

    The $n$th square number is $n^2$.
    $1^2 = 1$, $2^2 = 4$, $3^2 = 9$, and so on.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Triangular numbers
The sequence of triangular numbers is:

    $$1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, \dots$$

    These can be drawn as triangles of dots. Each term adds one more row than the previous term.
    $1 = 1$
    $3 = 1 + 2$
    $6 = 1 + 2 + 3$
    $10 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4$

💡 Worked Example 3 — Powers of 2
The sequence $2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, \dots$ is made by multiplying by $2$ each time.

    The $n$th term is $2^n$.
    $2^1 = 2$, $2^2 = 4$, $2^3 = 8$, and so on.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Square numbers: $1, 4, 9, 16, 25, \dots$ — $n$th term is $n^2$
• Triangular numbers: $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \dots$ — add $2, 3, 4, 5, \dots$ each time
• Powers of 2: $2, 4, 8, 16, 32, \dots$ — $n$th term is $2^n$

⚠️ Common Misconception
Thinking all sequences are arithmetic. Some sequences multiply, some square, and some change in more complicated ways. Always look at the pattern before choosing a rule.

notes.heading: Visual and Picture Patterns
notes.body:
Sequences can be shown with pictures, shapes, or dots. The same rules apply — you just need to turn the pictures into numbers first.

🔑 Key Concept
Count the objects in each picture to create a number sequence. Then find the term-to-term rule or the $n$th term rule.

💡 Worked Example
A pattern is made from squares.

  Picture 1: $1$ square
  Picture 2: $4$ squares
  Picture 3: $7$ squares
  Picture 4: $10$ squares

Find the number of squares in Picture 5 and write the $n$th term rule.

  Step 1: Write the number sequence
    $$1, 4, 7, 10, \dots$$

  Step 2: Find the common difference
    $4 - 1 = 3$
    $7 - 4 = 3$
    Rule: add $3$

  Step 3: Continue to Picture 5
    $10 + 3 = 13$

  Step 4: Find the $n$th term rule
    Common difference $= 3$, so start with $3n$
    When $n = 1$, $3n = 3$, but the first term is $1$
    $1 - 3 = -2$
    $$n\text{th term} = 3n - 2$$

  ✅ Check: For $n = 4$, $3(4) - 2 = 10$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Draw a table of picture number vs. count to organise the information
• The same methods work for number sequences and picture sequences
• Sketching the next picture can help you check your answer

✅ Tip
If a picture sequence grows by adding the same number each time, it has an arithmetic rule and the $n$th term will be $dn + c$.

notes.heading: Solving Sequence Problems
notes.body:
Many real-life problems can be modelled with sequences. Knowing how to find a rule and use it is a powerful problem-solving tool.

🔑 Key Concept
Word problems often describe an arithmetic pattern. Identify the first term and the common difference, then use the $n$th term rule.

💡 Worked Example — Word problem
A theatre has rows of seats. Row 1 has $12$ seats, Row 2 has $15$ seats, Row 3 has $18$ seats, and the pattern continues. How many seats are in Row 10?

  Step 1: Identify the sequence
    $$12, 15, 18, 21, \dots$$

  Step 2: Find the common difference
    $15 - 12 = 3$
    Common difference $d = 3$

  Step 3: Find the $n$th term rule
    Start with $3n$
    When $n = 1$, $3n = 3$, but the first term is $12$
    $12 - 3 = 9$
    $$n\text{th term} = 3n + 9$$

  Step 4: Substitute $n = 10$
    $3(10) + 9 = 30 + 9 = 39$

  ✅ Check: The sequence is $12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36, 39$. Row 10 has $39$ seats.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Read the problem carefully to find the first term and the common difference
• Write the $n$th term rule before substituting
• Check whether the question asks for a specific term, a rule, or a missing term

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the wrong value of $n$. Row 1 corresponds to $n = 1$, not $n = 0$. Always match the position to the question.

questions.stem: What is the next term in the sequence $3, 7, 11, 15, 19, \dots$?
questions.explanation: The rule is 'add $4$' because $7 - 3 = 4$, $11 - 7 = 4$, and so on. Therefore, $19 + 4 = 23$.

questions.stem: Find the missing term in the sequence $6, 10, \underline{\quad}, 18, 22$.
questions.explanation: Each term is $4$ more than the previous term, since $10 - 6 = 4$ and $22 - 18 = 4$. So $10 + 4 = 14$, and checking, $14 + 4 = 18$.

questions.stem: What is the term-to-term rule for the sequence $50, 45, 40, 35, 30, \dots$?
questions.explanation: Each term is $5$ less than the one before it, because $50 - 45 = 5$, $45 - 40 = 5$, and so on. The rule is 'subtract $5$'.

questions.stem: Which sequence follows the rule 'multiply by $2$'?
questions.explanation: In the sequence $2, 4, 8, 16, 32$, each term is double the previous term: $2 \times 2 = 4$, $4 \times 2 = 8$, and so on. That is 'multiply by $2$'.

questions.stem: What are the next two terms in the sequence $1, 5, 9, 13, 17, \dots$?
questions.explanation: The common difference is $4$, since $5 - 1 = 4$. Therefore, $17 + 4 = 21$, and $21 + 4 = 25$.

questions.stem: The $n$th term of a sequence is $5n + 1$. What is the $6$th term?
questions.explanation: Replace $n$ with $6$ in the rule $5n + 1$. First, $5 \times 6 = 30$, then add $1$ to get $31$.

questions.stem: What is the $n$th term rule for the sequence $4, 7, 10, 13, 16, \dots$?
questions.explanation: The common difference is $3$, so start with $3n$. When $n = 1$, $3n = 3$, but the first term is $4$, so add $1$. The rule is $3n + 1$.

questions.stem: Find the missing term in the sequence $24, 21, \underline{\quad}, 15, 12$.
questions.explanation: The rule is 'subtract $3$' because $24 - 21 = 3$ and $15 - 12 = 3$. So $21 - 3 = 18$, and checking, $18 - 3 = 15$.

questions.stem: Which of these is an arithmetic sequence?
questions.explanation: An arithmetic sequence has the same difference between each pair of terms. In $3, 6, 9, 12, 15$, the difference is always $3$, so it is arithmetic.

questions.stem: A picture pattern has $1$ dot, then $3$ dots, then $5$ dots, then $7$ dots. How many dots are in the $5$th picture?
questions.explanation: The number sequence is $1, 3, 5, 7$. The rule is 'add $2$', so the next term is $7 + 2 = 9$.

questions.stem: The $n$th term of a sequence is $4n - 2$. What is the first term?
questions.explanation: The first term uses $n = 1$. Calculate $4 \times 1 - 2$, which is $4 - 2 = 2$.

questions.stem: What is the $7$th term of the sequence that starts $2, 6, 10, 14, \dots$?
questions.explanation: The common difference is $4$, so the $n$th term is $4n - 2$. For the $7$th term, calculate $4 \times 7 - 2 = 28 - 2 = 26$.

questions.stem: A theatre has rows of seats. Row $1$ has $14$ seats, Row $2$ has $18$ seats, Row $3$ has $22$ seats, and the pattern continues. How many seats are in Row $8$?
questions.explanation: The sequence is $14, 18, 22, \dots$ with common difference $4$. The $n$th term is $4n + 10$. Substituting $n = 8$ gives $4(8) + 10 = 32 + 10 = 44$.

questions.stem: The $n$th term of a sequence is $3n + 7$. Which term equals $40$?
questions.explanation: Set $3n + 7 = 40$. Subtract $7$ to get $3n = 33$, then divide by $3$ to get $n = 11$. So the $11$th term is $40$.

questions.stem: A pattern made from squares has $1$ square in Picture $1$, $5$ squares in Picture $2$, $9$ squares in Picture $3$, and $13$ squares in Picture $4$. How many squares are in Picture $7$?
questions.explanation: The number sequence is $1, 5, 9, 13$, with common difference $4$. The $n$th term is $4n - 3$. For Picture $7$, $4(7) - 3 = 28 - 3 = 25$.
